title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Null Result on a Deterministic Synthetic Task Pool
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) that compares a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) pipeline to accepting an LLM suggestion directly for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a deterministic task generator and a deterministic validator, we sampled K=200 paired tasks and produced one shared generator output per task. Requested_model = gpt-5-mini. Primary outcome: regression‑causing change rate (validator failure) per arm. Observed: baseline 200/200 validator‑compliant applies, guarded 200/200; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap (10k, seed=1729) 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair path was never invoked (repair_applied = 0). We release complete preregistration (SHA‑256 a6d73a5c...), raw model/provider traces, validator traces, execution manifest (raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 3dfbe1b6...), and analysis artifacts to enable exact replay. We interpret the null as a ceiling case driven by the specific task/model/validator combination and discuss design implications for future confirmatory evaluations that aim to demonstrate verifier/repair utility in operationally realistic, failure‑rich regimes.

sections.introduction: Automated intent→configuration translation promises to accelerate change operations in networks but raises safety concerns because incorrect or out‑of‑sequence changes can cause service regressions. The generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) architectural pattern—an LLM generator followed by a deterministic verifier and a constrained repair step—has been proposed to reduce operator risk by catching and correcting unsafe proposals. However, the marginal operational benefit of adding a verifier+repair layer depends on (i) generator error profile, (ii) validator coverage and fidelity, and (iii) task distribution. To obtain a reproducible causal estimate of verifier marginal effect we preregistered a paired design that holds the generator output fixed and compares: (A) accept‑as‑is (LLM‑only baseline) versus (B) validator‑checked with an optional single repair attempt (guarded). The primary estimand was the paired difference in regression‑causing change rate (guarded minus baseline). All design choices, seeds, and analysis were frozen in the preregistration (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop; preregistration SHA‑256 a6d73a5c...). Key contributions: (1) a fully preregistered paired evaluation with deterministic sampling and archived artifacts; (2) a complete provenance bundle (model calls, provider traces, validator traces, and hashes) enabling exact replay; (3) a transparent empirical outcome (a ceiling/null case) and concrete guidance for subsequent confirmatory designs.
sections.related_work: The study is situated among recent work that (i) integrates LLMs into NetOps and AIOps for intent translation and configuration synthesis; (ii) proposes generate→validate→repair pipelines that combine generative models with deterministic verification; and (iii) argues for using formal or emulator‑based checkers as operational safeguards. Representative prior systems and benchmark efforts emphasize verifier utility when generator errors are common; our preregistered paired design complements that literature by isolating the verifier's marginal effect when generator outputs are identical across conditions. We used the closest verified literature to frame the experiment (see cited_record_ids). Unlike leaderboard-style multi‑model comparisons, our design prioritises causal identification and reproducibility via archived artifacts and deterministic selection.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and key parameters. The experiment was preregistered as study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop (SHA‑256 a6d73a5cc0bda22e...). Primary confirmatory hypothesis H1: the G→V→R (guarded) pipeline yields a lower regression‑causing change rate than the LLM‑only baseline (paired estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). Power assumptions (frozen): target absolute reduction = 0.08 assuming baseline regression rate ≈ 0.20; two‑sided α=0.05, power=0.80; bootstrap checks were preregistered for robustness. Sampling and task generation. Tasks derive deterministically from a public synthetic pool produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. To prevent selection bias we computed SHA‑256(intent_string), sorted ascending, and selected the first K=200 tasks that satisfied preregistered validator coverage. No human adjudication post‑lock; all exclusions and selection reasons are logged (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 f1d447b7...). Paired/ shared‑initial design. For each selected task we produced a single shared generator output candidate_c via the requested_model (gpt-5-mini). Baseline: candidate_c was the suggested apply. Guarded: candidate_c was first validated by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and only if validation failed an automated single repair call (max 1) to the same model was permitted; repaired candidate was revalidated once. This shared_initial_generation design isolates the verifier’s marginal effect by holding generator output identical across arms. Deterministic validator and scoring. The validator deterministically parses candidate text into structured commands and enforces policy/workflow rules (examples: shutdown_before_mtu_change, minimum_active_in_group, protected_interfaces). The scoring rule for the primary outcome was full_intent_constraint_validation (binary: valid==true/false). Validator traces record normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, final_state snapshot, violation codes, and valid boolean; these per‑episode traces are archived under execution/scoring/*.json (representative hashes in execution manifest). Model/provider configuration and call accounting. Requested_model recorded in execution/model_configuration.json (gpt-5-mini; SHA‑256 1acce92558ed...). The run used a shared generation per task (200 model calls total) and adhered to the preregistered maximum_model_calls=400. Provider traces and per‑call hashes are preserved in execution/provider_calls/*.json and execution/call_cache/*.json to detect caching or cross‑condition reuse. Statistical analysis. Primary confirmatory test: exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes (validator pass/fail). Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI used 10,000 resamples with seed=1729 (preregistered). Secondary estimands (time to deploy, model calls per success) were predeclared; they remained evaluable but became moot when repair was never invoked. Reproducibility controls. All artifacts, seeds, and cryptographic hashes are archived: raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 3dfbe1b6..., model_configuration.json SHA‑256 1acce9255..., preregistration SHA‑256 a6d73a5c..., master prompt provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 1872df1e...; full execution manifest enumerates all hashes for per‑episode artifacts (execution/execution_manifest.json).

sections.discussion: Interpretation: ceiling/null outcome. The observed perfect compliance in both arms is a legitimate experimental outcome: under our deterministic task sampling, model selection (gpt-5-mini), and validator coverage, the generator proposals satisfied all predeclared validator checks; therefore the verifier had no opportunity to change the binary apply outcome. This is a ceiling case that documents a regime in which G→V→R, as instantiated, yields no marginal benefit. Design implications for future confirmatory evaluations. To demonstrate verifier/repair utility within a confirmatory framework researchers should (i) select task pools with a nontrivial baseline error rate (historical failures, adversarially perturbed intents, or validator boundary cases); (ii) evaluate multiple generator strengths (include weaker models or parameter settings) to avoid ceiling effects; (iii) permit interactive generator–verifier adaptation (iterative generation in response to validator feedback) when the operational workflow expects such interplay; or (iv) alter the estimand to measure improvement in repair success conditional on initial validator failure. Our design intentionally fixed a single shared initial generation to isolate verifier marginal effect, but this choice also disallows generator adaptation to verifier feedback—an effect that can be operationally important. Threats to validity. Internal validity: maintained by deterministic sampling, frozen seeds, and comprehensive hash manifests. Construct validity: depends on how well deterministic_netops_validator_v5 maps to real operational regressions; if the validator omits realistic failure modes the primary outcome may not reflect operational safety. External validity: limited by single model (gpt-5-mini), synthetic deterministic tasks, and validator‑covered intents—results do not generalize to production task distributions or different model families. Conclusion validity: preregistered power targets assumed baseline failure ≈ 0.20; observed baseline = 1.0 invalidated those assumptions, producing a degenerate test statistic; we therefore present exact counts, exact McNemar p, and bootstrap CI rather than overinterpreting a power calculation. Operational implication. Practitioners should not infer that verifiers are unnecessary in production from this ceiling case. Instead, use the archived artifacts and diagnostics to design failure‑rich evaluations that reveal verifier value where it exists. Reproducibility and external reuse. We publish the complete artifact bundle and SHA‑256 manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json and referenced files). Replay recipe: (1) retrieve deterministic task generator and task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 f1d447b7...); (2) reproduce shared_initial_generation calls using archived provider_call traces and the same requested_model; (3) rerun deterministic_netops_validator_v5 on archived candidate texts and compare scoring traces (execution/scoring/*.json). The deterministic_reconciliation.json documents internal accounting and provider call audit consistency. Reviewer requests addressed. We explicitly report preregistered power assumptions and emphasize the shared_initial_generation limitation (which prohibits generator adaptation to verifier feedback) and suggest alternative interactive designs for future work.
sections.conclusion: A fully preregistered, paired evaluation comparing G→V→R to LLM‑only acceptance on K=200 deterministic NetOps tasks produced a null/ceiling outcome: both arms produced 200/200 validator‑compliant applies, paired difference = 0.00, exact McNemar p = 1.00, bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]; repair was never invoked. The result documents a regime where G→V→R provides no marginal benefit and highlights the importance of designing failure‑rich confirmatory evaluations. We release the full preregistration, execution traces, scoring artifacts, and hash manifests to enable exact replay and to guide future experiments that evaluate verifier and repair efficacy under operationally realistic failure patterns.

limitations: Single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize to other LLMs without additional experiments.
Synthetic deterministic task pool and deterministic sampling — external validity to production change intents and operator distributions is limited.
Primary outcome depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 fidelity to operational regressions; construct validity is tied to validator realism and coverage.
Ceiling effect: baseline success = 100% eliminated ability to demonstrate verifier/repair benefit under this design and sample.
Residual contamination (undetectable pretraining overlap) cannot be fully excluded despite hashing and logging; contamination_summary.csv recorded no flagged items for this run.
